lessons.title: Ethical, Cultural, Environmental and Privacy Impacts

before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark “Discuss Impacts” question, never list positives and negatives in two separate blocks. Each paragraph should make a point, give a specific example (name a technology and a group of people), acknowledge a counter-argument, and offer a judgement. End with a conclusion that states your overall view. Common mistakes include vague claims like “technology helps people” without naming which technology and which people — examiners want precision, not generalisation. Avoid single-sided answers; the 2024 examiners’ report flagged this as the most common reason for low scores on impacts questions.
before.content_html:
Technology and Society: A Double-Edged Sword

Digital technology has transformed every aspect of modern life — how we work, how we communicate, what we buy, and even how governments watch over us. Understanding these impacts is not just useful for the exam; it is essential for living and working in a digital world. The challenge is that most technologies bring both benefits and drawbacks, and a strong exam answer must weigh both sides honestly before reaching a judgement.

Ethical Issues

Ethics in computing refers to the moral questions that arise when technology affects people’s lives. Three issues appear regularly in extended-response questions: privacy, AI bias, and automation’s impact on employment.

Privacy. Every time you use a search engine, stream a video or post on social media, data about you is collected, analysed and often sold to advertisers. Digital privacy describes the right to control who can see and use that data. Many people accept these trade-offs knowingly; others do not realise how much information is being gathered. The ethical question is whether companies have a duty to limit data collection even when users technically “agree” to terms and conditions they have not read.

AI bias. Artificial intelligence systems are trained on data. If that data reflects existing social inequalities — for example, historical hiring decisions that undervalued women or certain ethnic groups — the AI can reproduce and even amplify those biases. A recruitment algorithm trained on past job-offer data may systematically score applications from women lower, even though the programmer never intended this. Ethically, developers have a responsibility to test their systems for bias and correct it before deployment.

Automation and employment. Robots and software now perform tasks that once required large human workforces: supermarket self-checkouts, warehouse picking robots, and automated customer-service chatbots. Supporters argue that automation creates new, higher-skilled jobs and raises overall productivity. Critics point out that the new jobs often go to people with degrees in technology, while factory and retail workers who lose their jobs lack the qualifications to move across. This widens inequality rather than reducing it.

Key Fact

Ethical issues in computing include privacy (data collected without meaningful consent), AI bias (systems that reflect and amplify existing social inequalities), and automation (displacing low-skilled workers while creating new high-skilled roles, widening inequality).

Cultural Issues

Digital technology has changed how cultures interact and how information spreads. Social media platforms allow people across the world to share ideas instantly, breaking down geographical barriers. However, the same tools have been linked to the spread of misinformation, online hate speech, and what researchers call a “filter bubble” — where algorithms show users content they already agree with, narrowing their worldview rather than broadening it.

The digital divide is a major cultural concern. In a society where government services, job applications, banking and education move online, people without reliable internet access or digital skills are increasingly excluded. The divide exists internationally (between high-income and low-income countries) and domestically (between urban and rural areas, and between older and younger generations). Bridging this gap is now seen as a matter of social justice.

Students often argue that technology is uniformly positive in extended-response answers. Examiners reward balanced reasoning. For every benefit (faster communication, access to information, remote working), there is a genuine drawback: not everyone can afford devices or data plans, older users may lack digital literacy, and rural areas often have poor connectivity. A top-band answer identifies a specific group who benefits and a specific group who does not, rather than making vague claims about “society.”

Environmental Issues

Computing’s environmental footprint is larger than most people realise. There are two main concerns: e-waste and energy consumption.

E-waste. The average smartphone is replaced every two to three years. Old devices often end up in landfill, where toxic materials — including lead, mercury, cadmium and lithium — can leach into soil and groundwater. Globally, e-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams. Responsible recycling schemes exist, but uptake is low because many consumers do not know where to take old devices.

Energy consumption. Data centres — the buildings that store and process cloud data — consume enormous quantities of electricity to power servers and keep them cool. It is estimated that data centres account for around 1% of global electricity consumption. The energy mix matters: data centres powered by renewable sources have a much lower carbon footprint than those powered by coal or gas. Cryptocurrency mining and training large AI models also require significant energy, raising questions about whether the benefits justify the environmental cost.

Key Fact

E-waste from discarded devices releases toxic substances including lead, mercury and cadmium. Data centres powering cloud services account for around 1% of global electricity use. Both issues mean computing has a significant — and often underestimated — environmental impact.

Privacy Issues and Surveillance

Governments and corporations have the technical ability to monitor individuals’ online behaviour in ways that were impossible a generation ago. CCTV cameras with facial-recognition software can track individuals through city streets. Internet service providers can log every website a user visits. Smartphones record location data continuously.

The ethical debate centres on where to draw the line between legitimate security and unacceptable intrusion. Law enforcement agencies argue that surveillance powers are essential for detecting terrorism and serious crime. Civil liberties organisations argue that mass surveillance — monitoring everyone rather than targeting suspects — chills free expression and presumes guilt rather than innocence.

Censorship is one of the most contested issues in digital society. Some governments block access to social media platforms, news websites or search results they consider threatening to political stability. Supporters argue that censorship protects citizens from dangerous misinformation, extremist content, and material harmful to children. Opponents argue that it violates the fundamental right to receive and share information freely, and that governments often censor political criticism alongside genuinely harmful content. In the UK, platforms are required to remove illegal content (such as terrorist material and child sexual abuse images), but legal content — including controversial political speech — is generally protected.

The debate over who should decide what is harmful is unresolved. Social media companies make content moderation decisions affecting billions of users, with limited external oversight. Whether these companies are best placed to make such judgements — or whether that role should belong to elected governments — is a genuinely open ethical question.

Writing a Balanced Extended Response

The 8-mark “Discuss Impacts” question is a regular feature of the exam. Examiners consistently penalise answers that list benefits in one paragraph and drawbacks in another without weighing them. A strong answer uses the following structure for each point: claim (what is the impact?) → evidence (which technology, which group?) → counter (who benefits differently or is harmed?) → judgement (on balance, is the impact positive or negative, and for whom?). Reaching a final conclusion that makes a supported overall judgement, even if tentative, is what separates a Mastering response from a Secure one.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Digital technology raises ethical issues including privacy (data collection without meaningful consent), AI bias (systems that amplify existing inequalities), and automation (displacing low-skilled workers while creating high-skilled roles).
  • Cultural impacts include the digital divide — unequal access to technology along lines of income, age and geography — and the risk of filter bubbles narrowing people’s worldviews.
  • Environmental costs include e-waste (toxic materials from discarded devices) and energy consumption (data centres account for around 1% of global electricity use). Extended-response answers must be balanced and conclude with a supported judgement.

before.content_html:
Why Does Computing Need Laws?

Technology moves faster than most people’s intuitions about right and wrong. Without legislation, individuals and organisations would have no clear boundaries for what is acceptable when handling personal data, accessing computer systems or copying digital content. UK law provides those boundaries through several key Acts of Parliament, each targeting a specific set of harms. You need to know the name, year, and purpose of each one.

Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR

The Data Protection Act 2018 is the main UK law governing the handling of personal data. It implements the requirements of the UK GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) into domestic law following Brexit. Any organisation that collects or processes personal data about living individuals must comply.

The Act gives individuals a set of key rights:

  • The right of access — you can request a copy of all personal data an organisation holds about you (a “Subject Access Request”).
  • The right to erasure — the “right to be forgotten”; you can ask an organisation to delete your data in certain circumstances.
  • The right to rectification — you can demand that inaccurate data about you is corrected.
  • The right to data portability — you can ask for your data in a machine-readable format to move it to another provider.

Organisations must have a lawful basis for processing data — such as your explicit consent, a contractual necessity, or a legal obligation. Data must be kept accurate, stored securely, and not retained longer than necessary. The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) enforces the Act and can issue large fines for breaches.

Key Fact

The Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR gives individuals four key rights: access (Subject Access Request), erasure (right to be forgotten), rectification (correct inaccurate data), and data portability. Organisations must have a lawful basis for any data processing.

Computer Misuse Act 1990

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 was introduced after two high-profile hacking cases revealed that UK law had no mechanism to prosecute people who accessed computer systems without permission. The Act created three principal offences:

  • Unauthorised access to computer material — hacking into a system you are not permitted to use, even if no data is taken. This is a summary offence, punishable by up to 2 years in prison.
  • Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence — hacking with the intention of committing fraud or blackmail. This carries a heavier penalty.
  • Unauthorised modification of computer material — changing, deleting or encrypting data without permission. This covers installing malware, ransomware, or deliberately corrupting files, and can carry up to 10 years in prison.

Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects creators’ intellectual property automatically from the moment a work is created — no registration is required. In computing, this means:

  • Copying or distributing software without a valid licence is illegal — this includes piracy of games, office software and creative tools.
  • Images, videos and music downloaded from the internet are typically protected — reusing them without permission or a licence is an infringement.
  • Code written by a developer is automatically their intellectual property (or their employer’s, if written during employment).

Creative Commons licences provide a legal framework for creators who want to share their work. Different Creative Commons licences allow different uses — for example, “Attribution” (CC BY) allows anyone to reuse the work as long as they credit the creator, while “Non-Commercial” (CC NC) restricts reuse to non-commercial purposes. Understanding which licence applies before reusing an image or piece of code is a key professional skill.

The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA) sets out when and how government agencies — such as the police, intelligence services and local councils — may lawfully intercept communications, use covert surveillance, and access electronic data. Before RIPA, there was no unified legal framework governing these powers; they were exercised under a patchwork of older laws.

RIPA requires that surveillance activities are authorised, necessary, and proportionate. For example, police can request that an internet service provider (ISP) retain records of a suspect’s online activity if a proper authorisation is in place. Without that authorisation, accessing such records would be unlawful. RIPA was later supplemented by the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 (sometimes called the “Snoopers’ Charter”), which updated and extended the framework for bulk data collection and equipment interference by intelligence services.

The Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOI Act) gives any person the right to request information held by public bodies — including government departments, local councils, NHS trusts and publicly funded schools. The public body must respond within 20 working days and either provide the information or explain why an exemption applies (for example, if disclosure would compromise national security or ongoing criminal investigations).

In computing terms, FOI requests are often used to obtain data about government IT contracts, software systems used in public services, or how personal data is managed. The Act promotes transparency and accountability, allowing journalists, researchers and ordinary citizens to scrutinise how public money and public power are being used.

Key Fact

Five key Acts and their years: Computer Misuse Act 1990, Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, Data Protection Act 2018 (UK GDPR), Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA), Freedom of Information Act 2000.

Professional Standards and Codes of Conduct

Laws set the minimum standard of behaviour. Professional standards go further — they describe what good practice looks like, even when the law does not require it. The British Computer Society (BCS) is the professional body for computing in the UK. Its Code of Conduct requires members to:

  • Act in the public interest — considering the broader impact of their work on society, not just the interests of their employer or client.
  • Maintain professional competence — keeping skills and knowledge up to date, and only taking on work they are qualified to do.
  • Act with integrity — being honest, avoiding conflicts of interest, and reporting concerns about unethical or dangerous software.
  • Respect the organisation and individuals — protecting confidential information, respecting colleagues, and not discriminating.

Codes of conduct like the BCS Code matter because computing professionals often work with sensitive data and critical infrastructure. A programmer who discovers that their employer’s software contains a serious security flaw has a professional obligation to raise the issue, even if doing so is inconvenient or commercially damaging. Professional codes provide a framework for making these ethical decisions — and, where the code is backed by a professional body, members who breach it can face disciplinary action including loss of membership.
